title: Siamese Abulug pomelo (Abulug pomelo): Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaTitle: Siamese Abulug pomelo: Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaDescription: Siamese Abulug pomelo is a pomelo variety. See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: Siamese Abulug is a registered pomelo variety, also sold or known as Abulug pomelo or NSIC Pm 04. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC) in 2008 as NSIC 2008 Pm 04. Celerina T. Miranda bred it. Its record notes a yield of 300 fruits/tree at 10 years.

blocks.text: If you came here looking for Abulug pomelo or NSIC Pm 04, this is the same pomelo. The facts below come from the NSIC registry kept by the Bureau of Plant Industry, with notes from its seller and farm sources. Compare it with the others in our [pomelo variety finder](/crop-varieties/pomelo), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [fertilizer for fruit trees](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. Its record notes a yield of 300 fruits/tree at 10 years. It bears every year. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

anee.io keeps the records of each block of trees, from fertilizer to harvest, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside them.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?
The registry gives no pest or disease ratings for this variety. So treat it as untested, and scout every week.

The pests and diseases that hit pomelo fields most often: [citrus greening](/diseases/citrus-greening), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug), [Oriental fruit fly](/pests/oriental-fruit-fly). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

The flesh is colorless to creamy white and soft. Its sweetness measured 10.5 degrees Brix, the share of sugar in the juice. Most table fruit tastes sweet from about 12 Brix up. The edible part is 53.8 percent of the fruit.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Yield:** About 300 fruits per tree at 10 years.
**Fruit:** Round, greenish to light yellow peel, very juicy, sweet, colorless to creamy white flesh, about 10.5 Brix, seedy (about 59 seeds).

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: a heavy bearing Cagayan Valley pomelo: about 300 fruits per tree at 10 years. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant Siamese Abulug pomelo

Davao is the home of suha. Pick a registered selection by flesh color and sweetness, and plant marcotted trees. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Land preparation for fruit trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is Abulug pomelo the same as Siamese Abulug?
items.a: Yes. Abulug pomelo is another name for Siamese Abulug, registered as NSIC 2008 Pm 04. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.
The record shows a recorded yield of 300 fruits/tree at 10 years. Your own yield depends on the soil, water, fertilizer and pests on your farm.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of Siamese Abulug?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
